the act of using the Internet itself may result in overestimation of one’s ability and performance, but that this overestimation is not a persistent side effect of Internet technology use, but rather an effect of the act of searching the Internet.
Internet use results in better answers, and in significant and persistent, but not necessarily accurate, overestimation of ability and performance.
the use of the Internet for searching for information on a specific task increases overestimation of one’s own information problem-solving ability, even in postdictive judgments.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of the Internet as an information source on the metacognitive processes of the user.
the consequences of using the Internet for information problem solving.
the effects of Internet use on users’ metacognitive knowledge and judgments and the potential consequences of these effects for users’ information problem-solving behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Internet use is associated with overestimation of ability and performance, but that this effect does not generalize across tasks and phases.
Internet use does increase overestimation of one’s own information problem-solving ability, and this overestimation is persistent.
Internet use increases overestimation of one’s own information problem-solving ability, but not necessarily of one’s own performance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Internet users are prone to overestimating their ability or performance.
Internet use may lead users to overestimate themselves, which may in turn result in premature termination of information search, suboptimal performance, and other negative outcomes.
the Internet is not only a useful tool to find information, but that it can be used as a tool to improve one’s own metacognitive judgments and self-assessments.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the act of using the Internet to search for information itself may bias users’ metacognitive judgments toward overestimation.
the Internet may be a double-edged sword, and that its benefits may come with costs.
